sections.label: Analytical scope
sections.statement: CARTA's Loire Valley is an analytical wine corridor from the Pays Nantais through Anjou, Saumur and Touraine to Centre-Loire, with the Vallée du Loir retained as a tributary branch. It is not a single legal wine area and has no standalone regulatory polygon.

sections.label: Component places
sections.statement: For Atlas navigation the Loire corridor is resolved into Pays Nantais, Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Centre-Loire, with Vallée du Loir as a visible northern tributary branch; these are analytical components rather than a fabricated legal hierarchy.

The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.

sections.label: Physical transition
sections.statement: The corridor moves from the crystalline Armorican context of the Nantais through Anjou schist and the tuffeau/chalk country of Saumur and Touraine toward the sedimentary hills of Centre-Loire. The Loire connects these transitions but does not erase them.

sections.label: Why Loire matters
sections.statement: Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.

sections.label: How to read the place
sections.statement: Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

sections.label: River network
sections.statement: The Loire is the main corridor, while the Sèvre Nantaise, Layon, Vienne, Cher and Loir provide distinct tributary routes through the wine world. The Loir is a different river from the Loire.

sections.label: People and lineages
sections.statement: Loire producer history is not one natural-wine school: documented routes include family succession, biodynamic advocacy, work and collaboration, ownership change, estate/négociant separation and appellation disputes across different component places.

sections.label: Legal layers
sections.statement: Current AOP regulatory areas, the Val de Loire IGP, InterLoire's institutional operating scope, UNESCO's Loire cultural landscape and CARTA's analytical Loire Valley are different objects and must not be used as substitute boundaries for one another.

sections.statement: Béarn is the historical and cultural foothill world around Pau; CARTA keeps it distinct from Béarn AOP and uses Jurançon as the clearest mapped route into its white-wine culture.

sections.label: Why this world matters
sections.statement: The Béarn–Jurançon world makes the relationship between mountain foothills, long autumn ripening, local Manseng grapes and both dry and sweet white wine unusually legible.

sections.label: Jurançon landscape
sections.statement: INAO describes hillside vineyards in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence, with a warm dry southerly autumn wind that can support ripening and concentration.

sections.label: Dry + sweet
sections.statement: Jurançon includes dry and sweet white-wine traditions centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng; sweetness is a style distinction inside the appellation, not a different geography.

sections.label: Three legal paths
sections.statement: The current Jurançon specification distinguishes three white-wine paths in the same geography: Jurançon sec at no more than 4 grams per litre of fermentable sugars, Jurançon above 40 grams per litre, and Jurançon vendanges tardives above 55 grams per litre.

sections.label: Principal + accessory grapes
sections.statement: The current Jurançon specification names Gros Manseng and Petit Manseng as principal varieties and Camaralet de Lasseube, Courbu, Lauzet and Petit Courbu as accessory varieties; the vendanges tardives mention is reserved to the two Mansengs.

sections.label: Harvest changes the path
sections.statement: All Jurançon grapes are hand harvested. Successive picking passes are required except for Jurançon sec, while vendanges tardives fruit cannot be harvested before 2 November; off-vine passerillage is prohibited apart from handling within the parcel during harvest.

sections.label: Why ripeness keeps freshness
sections.statement: Jurançon’s wet Atlantic foothills are tempered in autumn by a frequent warm, dry southerly foehn. On steep slopes and terraces, late, thick-skinned local grapes can concentrate while retaining high acidity and resisting grey rot, which helps explain how dry, sweet and late-harvest wines remain distinct paths rather than different places.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.label: Analytical scope
sections.statement: CARTA's Loire Valley is an analytical wine corridor from the Pays Nantais through Anjou, Saumur and Touraine to Centre-Loire, with the Vallée du Loir retained as a tributary branch. It is not a single legal wine area and has no standalone regulatory polygon.

sections.label: Component places
sections.statement: For Atlas navigation the Loire corridor is resolved into Pays Nantais, Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Centre-Loire, with Vallée du Loir as a visible northern tributary branch; these are analytical components rather than a fabricated legal hierarchy.

The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.

sections.label: Physical transition
sections.statement: The corridor moves from the crystalline Armorican context of the Nantais through Anjou schist and the tuffeau/chalk country of Saumur and Touraine toward the sedimentary hills of Centre-Loire. The Loire connects these transitions but does not erase them.

sections.label: Why Loire matters
sections.statement: Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.

sections.label: How to read the place
sections.statement: Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

sections.label: River network
sections.statement: The Loire is the main corridor, while the Sèvre Nantaise, Layon, Vienne, Cher and Loir provide distinct tributary routes through the wine world. The Loir is a different river from the Loire.

sections.label: People and lineages
sections.statement: Loire producer history is not one natural-wine school: documented routes include family succession, biodynamic advocacy, work and collaboration, ownership change, estate/négociant separation and appellation disputes across different component places.

sections.label: Legal layers
sections.statement: Current AOP regulatory areas, the Val de Loire IGP, InterLoire's institutional operating scope, UNESCO's Loire cultural landscape and CARTA's analytical Loire Valley are different objects and must not be used as substitute boundaries for one another.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.statement: Jurançon is a Pyrenean-foothill white-wine AOP centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng, with established dry and sweet traditions.

sections.label: Jurançon landscape
sections.statement: INAO describes hillside vineyards in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence, with a warm dry southerly autumn wind that can support ripening and concentration.

sections.label: Dry + sweet
sections.statement: Jurançon includes dry and sweet white-wine traditions centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng; sweetness is a style distinction inside the appellation, not a different geography.

sections.label: Three legal paths
sections.statement: The current Jurançon specification distinguishes three white-wine paths in the same geography: Jurançon sec at no more than 4 grams per litre of fermentable sugars, Jurançon above 40 grams per litre, and Jurançon vendanges tardives above 55 grams per litre.

sections.label: Principal + accessory grapes
sections.statement: The current Jurançon specification names Gros Manseng and Petit Manseng as principal varieties and Camaralet de Lasseube, Courbu, Lauzet and Petit Courbu as accessory varieties; the vendanges tardives mention is reserved to the two Mansengs.

sections.label: Harvest changes the path
sections.statement: All Jurançon grapes are hand harvested. Successive picking passes are required except for Jurançon sec, while vendanges tardives fruit cannot be harvested before 2 November; off-vine passerillage is prohibited apart from handling within the parcel during harvest.

sections.label: Why ripeness keeps freshness
sections.statement: Jurançon’s wet Atlantic foothills are tempered in autumn by a frequent warm, dry southerly foehn. On steep slopes and terraces, late, thick-skinned local grapes can concentrate while retaining high acidity and resisting grey rot, which helps explain how dry, sweet and late-harvest wines remain distinct paths rather than different places.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.label: Analytical scope
sections.statement: CARTA's Loire Valley is an analytical wine corridor from the Pays Nantais through Anjou, Saumur and Touraine to Centre-Loire, with the Vallée du Loir retained as a tributary branch. It is not a single legal wine area and has no standalone regulatory polygon.

sections.label: Component places
sections.statement: For Atlas navigation the Loire corridor is resolved into Pays Nantais, Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Centre-Loire, with Vallée du Loir as a visible northern tributary branch; these are analytical components rather than a fabricated legal hierarchy.

The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.

sections.label: Physical transition
sections.statement: The corridor moves from the crystalline Armorican context of the Nantais through Anjou schist and the tuffeau/chalk country of Saumur and Touraine toward the sedimentary hills of Centre-Loire. The Loire connects these transitions but does not erase them.

sections.label: Why Loire matters
sections.statement: Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.

sections.label: How to read the place
sections.statement: Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

sections.label: River network
sections.statement: The Loire is the main corridor, while the Sèvre Nantaise, Layon, Vienne, Cher and Loir provide distinct tributary routes through the wine world. The Loir is a different river from the Loire.

sections.label: People and lineages
sections.statement: Loire producer history is not one natural-wine school: documented routes include family succession, biodynamic advocacy, work and collaboration, ownership change, estate/négociant separation and appellation disputes across different component places.

sections.label: Legal layers
sections.statement: Current AOP regulatory areas, the Val de Loire IGP, InterLoire's institutional operating scope, UNESCO's Loire cultural landscape and CARTA's analytical Loire Valley are different objects and must not be used as substitute boundaries for one another.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.statement: Béarn is the historical and cultural foothill world around Pau; CARTA keeps it distinct from Béarn AOP and uses Jurançon as the clearest mapped route into its white-wine culture.

sections.label: Why this world matters
sections.statement: The Béarn–Jurançon world makes the relationship between mountain foothills, long autumn ripening, local Manseng grapes and both dry and sweet white wine unusually legible.

sections.label: Jurançon landscape
sections.statement: INAO describes hillside vineyards in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence, with a warm dry southerly autumn wind that can support ripening and concentration.

sections.label: Dry + sweet
sections.statement: Jurançon includes dry and sweet white-wine traditions centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng; sweetness is a style distinction inside the appellation, not a different geography.

sections.label: Three legal paths
sections.statement: The current Jurançon specification distinguishes three white-wine paths in the same geography: Jurançon sec at no more than 4 grams per litre of fermentable sugars, Jurançon above 40 grams per litre, and Jurançon vendanges tardives above 55 grams per litre.

sections.label: Principal + accessory grapes
sections.statement: The current Jurançon specification names Gros Manseng and Petit Manseng as principal varieties and Camaralet de Lasseube, Courbu, Lauzet and Petit Courbu as accessory varieties; the vendanges tardives mention is reserved to the two Mansengs.

sections.label: Harvest changes the path
sections.statement: All Jurançon grapes are hand harvested. Successive picking passes are required except for Jurançon sec, while vendanges tardives fruit cannot be harvested before 2 November; off-vine passerillage is prohibited apart from handling within the parcel during harvest.

sections.label: Why ripeness keeps freshness
sections.statement: Jurançon’s wet Atlantic foothills are tempered in autumn by a frequent warm, dry southerly foehn. On steep slopes and terraces, late, thick-skinned local grapes can concentrate while retaining high acidity and resisting grey rot, which helps explain how dry, sweet and late-harvest wines remain distinct paths rather than different places.

sections.label: Current legal structure
sections.statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

sections.label: Beaujolais now
sections.statement: Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.

sections.label: A long wine corridor
sections.statement: The August 2026 specification describes the Beaujolais wine area as a north–south corridor about 55 kilometres long and 15–20 kilometres wide, with the Saône plain to the east, the Monts du Beaujolais to the west and a regional landscape roughly 180–550 metres in elevation.

sections.label: Ten crus
sections.statement: The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

sections.label: Why Beaujolais matters
sections.statement: The 2024 institutional picture shows how one dominant grape can still yield distinct places: the Beaujolais and Villages production areas provide broad context around ten individually named crus.

sections.label: A varied physical place
sections.statement: Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

sections.label: North and south are not one rock story
sections.statement: The current specification distinguishes an older northern geological family dominated by Paleozoic granite, schist, metamorphic and volcano-sedimentary formations from younger Triassic and Jurassic sedimentary formations that become important in southern Beaujolais; official terroir research also shows substantial variation within that shorthand.

sections.statement: Jura is a compact eastern French wine region whose six wine AOPs form three overlapping families: geographic still-wine origins, traditional-method Crémant du Jura, and fortified Macvin du Jura.

sections.label: Why Jura matters
sections.statement: Jura makes legal hierarchy, grape identity and winemaking method unusually easy to compare in one small place: Chardonnay and Savagnin whites, three red grapes, vin jaune, sparkling wine and mistelle all coexist without meaning the same thing.

sections.label: Physical place
sections.statement: The Jura vineyard forms a narrow north–south band along the western foothills of the Jura mountains, with varied slopes and exposures rather than one uniform site.

sections.label: How to read the hierarchy
sections.statement: Arbois, Côtes du Jura, L’Etoile and Château-Chalon are geographic AOPs; Crémant du Jura and Macvin du Jura overlap that geography but govern different wine categories and methods.

sections.label: The wine picture
sections.statement: Côtes du Jura permits white, red, rosé and vin jaune; Crémant du Jura is traditional-method sparkling wine; Macvin du Jura is a white, red or rosé liqueur wine. These are distinct legal styles, not interchangeable labels.

sections.label: Analytical scope
sections.statement: CARTA's Loire Valley is an analytical wine corridor from the Pays Nantais through Anjou, Saumur and Touraine to Centre-Loire, with the Vallée du Loir retained as a tributary branch. It is not a single legal wine area and has no standalone regulatory polygon.

sections.label: Component places
sections.statement: For Atlas navigation the Loire corridor is resolved into Pays Nantais, Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Centre-Loire, with Vallée du Loir as a visible northern tributary branch; these are analytical components rather than a fabricated legal hierarchy.

The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.

sections.label: Physical transition
sections.statement: The corridor moves from the crystalline Armorican context of the Nantais through Anjou schist and the tuffeau/chalk country of Saumur and Touraine toward the sedimentary hills of Centre-Loire. The Loire connects these transitions but does not erase them.

sections.label: Why Loire matters
sections.statement: Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.

sections.label: How to read the place
sections.statement: Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

sections.label: River network
sections.statement: The Loire is the main corridor, while the Sèvre Nantaise, Layon, Vienne, Cher and Loir provide distinct tributary routes through the wine world. The Loir is a different river from the Loire.

sections.label: People and lineages
sections.statement: Loire producer history is not one natural-wine school: documented routes include family succession, biodynamic advocacy, work and collaboration, ownership change, estate/négociant separation and appellation disputes across different component places.

sections.label: Legal layers
sections.statement: Current AOP regulatory areas, the Val de Loire IGP, InterLoire's institutional operating scope, UNESCO's Loire cultural landscape and CARTA's analytical Loire Valley are different objects and must not be used as substitute boundaries for one another.
